title: BC Mineral Titles Online (MTO): How to Find, Map and Monitor Mineral Claims
metaDescription: What Mineral Titles Online is, what it is the authority for, and how to search, map and monitor British Columbia mineral claims — including where Exploration Maps helps and where you still need MTO.
cardSummary: What MTO is, what it is authoritative for, and how to search, map and monitor BC mineral claims around it.
directAnswer: Mineral Titles Online (MTO) is the Province of British Columbia's official system for acquiring and administering mineral, placer and coal titles. It is where claims are staked, maintained, transferred and paid for, and it is the authoritative record of who holds a title and when it expires. Exploration Maps does not replace MTO — it reads the province's public tenure dataset so you can search claims by tenure number or registered owner, map them, and track good-to-dates, then sends you back to MTO for anything that governs a transaction or a deadline.

ctaTop.text: Search BC claims by tenure number or owner.
ctaTop.sub: Map them in a couple of minutes, then verify in MTO.

ctaBottom.text: Monitor up to 10 BC claims free.
ctaBottom.sub: Reminders at 90, 30 and 1 day before each good-to-date.

sections.h2: What Mineral Titles Online actually is
sections.body: MTO is the Province of British Columbia's online system for mineral, placer and coal titles, run by the Mineral Titles Branch. It is a transactional system, not just a viewer: free miner certificate holders use it to acquire cell claims, register assessment work, pay cash in lieu, apply for leases, and transfer title.
sections.html: That transactional role is why MTO is the authority. A tenure's current status, its good-to-date, its registered owner and its boundaries are what MTO says they are. Any other source — including this one — is a copy of published data, and a copy can be stale, partial, or wrong. Start at Mineral Titles Online; background, rules and contacts are on the Mineral Titles Branch site.

box.title: What must be verified in MTO
box.html: Current ownership, current status, good-to-date, and exact boundaries — before any transaction, filing, staking decision or deadline decision. Exploration Maps is not the official title registry and does not connect to your MTO account.

sections.h2: What people actually use MTO for
items: Acquiring cell claims (which requires a free miner certificate and an MTO account)
Registering statements of work, or paying cash in lieu, to push a good-to-date forward
Transferring title, and recording ownership changes
Applying for mineral or placer leases
Checking the authoritative status and expiry of a specific tenure number
sections.body: Every one of those is a transaction or an authoritative lookup, and every one of them happens in MTO. Nothing in this guide changes that.

sections.h2: Where MTO is hard work, and what to do instead
sections.body: MTO is built for administering titles, not for exploring the tenure landscape. Three jobs are noticeably awkward in it:
items: Seeing a whole company's land position at once, rather than one tenure at a time
Getting claim boundaries out as a map you can put in a deck, a report or a news release
Remembering, months later, that a good-to-date is approaching
sections.html: Those three gaps are what Exploration Maps is for. It reads the province's public mineral tenure dataset — the same DataBC layer that underlies most third-party BC claim maps — and puts a search, a map and a reminder system on top of it.

sections.h2: Searching BC claims outside MTO
sections.body: In Exploration Maps, open Add Claims → Search Claims Registry and select British Columbia. Three search modes are available for BC:

rows: You want a company's whole BC land position
You have a specific claim in hand
You are working a NTS map area

sections.html: Owner search returns candidates grouped by match confidence rather than a finished answer, because company names reach the registry in clipped legal form, under previous names, and through subsidiaries and joint-venture partners. You confirm what enters your map. The company claim-search guide covers that workflow in detail.

sections.h2: Mapping the results
sections.body: Select the tenures you want and add them to the map. They come in as a claims layer with the boundaries from the public dataset, and the map fits to their extent. Assign the Claims role for the blue stroke and semi-transparent fill convention that most NI 43-101 figures use, add a title block and your logo, and export.
sections.html: If you already have a tenure file from MTO or a GIS, import it instead — GeoJSON, zipped Shapefile and KML all work. See how to map BC mineral claims from the public registry for the full walkthrough.

sections.h2: Tracking good-to-dates afterwards
sections.body: The good-to-date is the date by which a claim must be maintained — assessment work recorded, or cash paid in lieu — to stay in good standing. MTO is where you do that work. Exploration Maps is where you find out it is coming.
sections.html: Tenure Monitor saves a group of claims, reads their published good-to-dates, and emails reminders at 90, 30 and 1 day beforehand. It also flags changes it detects in the government record — a good-to-date that moved, an owner added or removed, a title that stopped appearing in the dataset. See the BC claim expiry guide.

cta.sub: Reminders before each good-to-date. No credit card.

sections.h2: How current the public data is
sections.body: Exploration Maps synchronizes the province's published tenure dataset on a schedule and displays the timestamp of the last successful synchronization on every portfolio view and in every reminder email. The province does not document an update frequency for the published dataset, so nothing here is described as live.

box.title: Data source
box.html: BC mineral tenure data is published by DataBC. Contains information licensed under the Open Government Licence – British Columbia. Published data is a copy of the registry, not the registry.

sections.h2: When to go back to MTO
items: Before staking, or deciding not to re-stake ground
Before filing assessment work or paying cash in lieu
Before any transaction — option, purchase, transfer, or JV
When a reminder or a detected change tells you something moved
Any time the exact boundary or the exact expiry date matters
sections.body: The short version: use Exploration Maps to notice things and to communicate them, and use MTO to decide and to act.

faqs.q: What is Mineral Titles Online?
faqs.a: MTO is the Province of British Columbia's official online system for mineral, placer and coal titles, administered by the Mineral Titles Branch. Free miner certificate holders use it to acquire cell claims, register assessment work, pay cash in lieu, transfer title and apply for leases. It is the authoritative record of BC mineral title.

faqs.q: Do I need a free miner certificate to search BC mineral claims?
faqs.a: No. A free miner certificate is required to acquire and hold mineral title in British Columbia, and to transact in MTO. Searching and viewing published tenure information — including in Exploration Maps — does not require one.

faqs.q: Can Exploration Maps replace MTO?
faqs.a: No, and it is not intended to. Exploration Maps reads the province's published tenure dataset to make searching, mapping and deadline tracking easier. It does not log into MTO, store MTO credentials, file assessment work, pay cash in lieu, register title, or acquire ground. Ownership, status, boundaries and deadlines must be verified in MTO.

faqs.q: How do I find who owns a mineral claim in BC?
faqs.a: Search by registered owner in Exploration Maps to see a company's published land position, or look up a specific tenure number. For authoritative ownership — the answer you would rely on for a transaction — check the tenure in MTO, which is the registry of record.

faqs.q: Is the claim data in Exploration Maps live?
faqs.a: No. It reflects the last successful synchronization with the province's published dataset, and that timestamp is shown on every portfolio view and in every reminder email. Tenure status can change, so verify anything that matters in MTO.

faqs.q: What is a good-to-date?
faqs.a: The date by which a mineral claim must be maintained — through recorded assessment work or a cash payment in lieu — to remain in good standing. It is published in the BC tenure dataset and is the date Tenure Monitor counts down to, in Pacific time.

title: How to Find Mineral Claims Owned by a Company in British Columbia
metaDescription: Search BC mineral claims by registered owner to see a company's land position — for competitor research, project generation, due diligence and neighbouring-ground checks. Verify ownership in MTO.
cardSummary: Search by registered owner to see a company's BC land position — competitor research, project generation and due diligence.
directAnswer: To find mineral claims held by a company in British Columbia, search the province's published tenure data by registered owner. In Exploration Maps, open Add Claims → Search Claims Registry, select British Columbia, choose the registered-owner mode and enter the company name. Matches are returned as candidates grouped by confidence — company names reach the registry in clipped legal form and under previous names — so you confirm which titles are actually theirs before mapping them. Authoritative ownership must be confirmed in Mineral Titles Online.

ctaTop.text: See a company's BC land position.
ctaTop.sub: Search by registered owner, select the matches, map them.

ctaBottom.text: Map a competitor's ground in a few minutes.
ctaBottom.sub: Then watch it — Tenure Monitor tracks claims you don't own.

sections.h2: Why you would want this
sections.body: Owner search answers a question that is genuinely hard to answer one tenure at a time.

rows: How much ground a peer holds, where it is, and how it has moved
Who holds the ground around a showing or a geophysical anomaly
Whether a vendor's claimed land position matches the published record
Who you actually share a boundary with before you approach anyone
Your own holdings, assembled in one view rather than tenure by tenure

sections.h2: The search, step by step
sections.body: Open Exploration Maps and choose Add Claims → Search Claims Registry. Select British Columbia, choose the registered-owner mode, and type the company name. Start with the distinctive part of the name rather than the full legal form — 'Goliath' will find more than 'Goliath Resources Limited' if the registry recorded it differently.

image.alt: Claim search panel with British Columbia selected and a company name entered
image.caption: Searching BC tenures by registered owner

sections.h2: Read the candidates properly
sections.body: Results come back grouped: exact name match, possible match, and weak match. That grouping is deliberate and it is worth respecting.
sections.html: Company names reach a title registry in clipped legal form, with inconsistent punctuation, under previous corporate names, through numbered subsidiaries, and in the name of one joint-venture partner rather than the operator everyone talks about. A name match ranks a candidate; it does not establish who holds the ground. Nothing enters your map until you tick it.

box.title: What a name match is and is not
box.html: Owner search matches the registered-owner field in the province's published tenure data. It is a search aid. It is not a determination of legal ownership, and a company's real land position may include titles held under a name you did not search. Confirm ownership in Mineral Titles Online.

sections.h2: Select the whole position at once
sections.body: Each candidate group has a select-all control, and the footer totals what you have selected — claim count and hectares together. Those two numbers are the land position, and they are the numbers you will end up quoting, so it is worth reading them before you add rather than counting rows afterwards.
sections.html: Hectares in particular tends to surprise people: forty small cell claims and four large leases can describe very different companies.

sections.h2: Map it
sections.body: Add the selected tenures and the map fits to their extent. Assign the Claims role for standard styling, and give the layer a name that will read in the legend — 'Peer Ground' or 'Optioned Claims' rather than the default. If you are comparing two companies, add each as its own layer with different stroke colours; they become separate legend entries automatically.

sections.h2: Watch ground you don't own
sections.body: A monitored group of claims is a watch list, not an ownership record. You can add a competitor's titles to it and get told when the published record for them changes — a good-to-date that moved, an owner added or removed, a title that stopped appearing in the dataset.
sections.html: That is often more useful than the initial search. A neighbour's claim reaching its good-to-date, or changing hands, is exactly the kind of event you would rather learn about early. Nothing about monitoring is visible to the title holder, and nothing about it changes the title.

box.title: A change is not an opportunity until you have checked
box.html: A status change, a termination date, or a title dropping out of the published dataset is what the published data shows. It is not confirmation that ground is available. Records leave a published dataset for several reasons, including partial publication at the province. Check the tenure in MTO before acting on it.

cta.text: Monitor up to 10 BC claims free.
cta.sub: Yours or anybody's. Reminders before each good-to-date.

sections.h2: Where this workflow stops
items: It reflects published data as of the last successful synchronization, not the live registry
It matches a registered-owner field, so beneficial ownership and option agreements are invisible to it
It cannot tell you about applications in progress beyond what the province publishes
It is not a substitute for a title search when money is changing hands
sections.body: For a transaction, use it to build the picture and then verify every tenure in MTO.

faqs.q: Can I search BC mineral claims by company name?
faqs.a: Yes. Exploration Maps searches the province's published tenure data by registered owner and returns candidates grouped by match confidence. Company names are often recorded in clipped legal form, so try the distinctive part of the name on its own. Confirm ownership in Mineral Titles Online before relying on it.

faqs.q: How do I find out who owns a mineral claim in BC?
faqs.a: Look up the tenure number — in Exploration Maps for the published registered owner and a map of the boundary, or in Mineral Titles Online for the authoritative record. For anything that governs a transaction, MTO is the answer that counts.

faqs.q: Can I see a competitor's whole land position?
faqs.a: You can see the titles published under a registered-owner name matching your search, with a claim count and total hectares. That is usually most of it, but it will miss ground held under a subsidiary, a previous corporate name, or a joint-venture partner's name — so treat the result as a strong starting point rather than a complete answer.

faqs.q: Is it legal to look up another company's mineral claims?
faqs.a: Yes. BC mineral tenure information is public data published by the province under the Open Government Licence – British Columbia. Searching, mapping and monitoring it is ordinary competitive research, and nothing about doing so is visible to the title holder.

faqs.q: Can I monitor claims that belong to someone else?
faqs.a: Yes. A monitored group is a watch list rather than an ownership record, so a competitor's ground, a property you are evaluating, or a block next to your own can all be added and tracked with the same reminders as your own claims.

directAnswer: Each Canadian province and territory runs its own mineral tenure registry, and they differ in what they publish. Exploration Maps supports direct claim search for British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Newfoundland & Labrador and Yukon. All seven can be mapped. Tenure Monitor — saved claim groups with good-to-date reminders and change detection — currently covers British Columbia only. Every jurisdiction's official registry remains the authority for ownership, status and boundaries.

ctaTop.sub: Pick a province, search by owner or claim number, map the result.

ctaBottom.sub: Search a province, add the claims, export a map.

sections.h2: What each registry is, and what we support
sections.body: The table below reflects what the application actually does today. Where a column says no, it means the capability does not exist yet — not that it is coming.
sections.html: Manitoba: the public disposition layer does not publish a holder name, so only claim-number lookup is offered. That is a limit of the published data rather than a decision on our side, and it is the reason the Manitoba guide leads with the claim number.

sections.h2: The jurisdiction guides
sections.body: Where a province has enough of its own quirks to be worth its own walkthrough, it has one:
sections.html:
• British Columbia — owner, tenure number and map-sheet search, plus the strongest tenure tooling on the site
  • Ontario — MLAS cell claims and how holder names are recorded
  • Quebec — GESTIM claims (claims désignés sur carte) and titleholder search
  • Saskatchewan — MARS dispositions
  • Manitoba — claim-number lookup, and why owner search is unavailable
  • Newfoundland & Labrador — licences rather than claims, and what that changes
Yukon — quartz claims only; placer is a separate register

sections.h2: Why the registries differ so much
sections.body: Mineral tenure is administered provincially and territorially in Canada, so there is no national claim registry and no common data model. The practical consequences show up quickly:
items: The unit of tenure differs — claims, cells, licences, dispositions and leases are not interchangeable terms
Holder or owner information is published in some jurisdictions and withheld in others
Expiry works differently: BC's good-to-date is not the same instrument as an anniversary date elsewhere
Boundary precision and coordinate reference systems vary by source
Update frequency for published datasets is often undocumented
sections.html: This is why the guides are per-jurisdiction rather than one generic article. A single "how to search Canadian mining claims" page would have to be vague enough to be useless.

sections.h2: What to verify, wherever you are working

box.title: The registry governs
box.html: Exploration Maps reads published tenure data and is not an official registry in any jurisdiction. Ownership, status, expiry and exact boundaries must be verified with the responsible provincial or territorial registry before a transaction, a filing, or a deadline decision.

sections.body: Published datasets are copies. They can lag the registry, omit recent transactions, or carry generalized boundaries. That is manageable as long as you know which questions require the authoritative source — and all of the expensive ones do.

sections.h2: Tenure monitoring, and why it is BC-first
sections.body: Tenure Monitor tracks good-to-dates, sends reminders before them, and detects changes in the published record. It covers British Columbia only at present.
sections.html: The reason is that BC publishes a good-to-date as a structured field on every title, which is what makes a reliable countdown possible. Other jurisdictions express maintenance obligations differently, and building a reminder system on a date we had to infer would be building a reminder system that is sometimes wrong about a deadline — which is worse than not having one. See the BC good-to-date guide.

faqs.q: Is there a national mineral claim registry in Canada?
faqs.a: No. Mineral tenure is administered by each province and territory, so there is no single national registry and no common data format. Each jurisdiction runs its own system — MTO in British Columbia, MLAS in Ontario, GESTIM in Quebec, MARS in Saskatchewan, and so on.

faqs.q: Which Canadian jurisdictions can I search in Exploration Maps?
faqs.a: British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Newfoundland & Labrador and Yukon. All seven support claim-number lookup and all but Manitoba support owner search — Manitoba's public layer does not publish a holder name.

faqs.q: Can I monitor claim expiry outside British Columbia?
faqs.a: Not yet. Tenure Monitor covers British Columbia only, because BC publishes a good-to-date as a structured field on every title. Other jurisdictions express maintenance obligations differently, and a countdown built on an inferred date would sometimes be wrong about a deadline.

faqs.q: Why can't I search Manitoba claims by company?
faqs.a: Manitoba's public mineral disposition layer does not publish a holder name field, so there is nothing to match a company against. Claim-number lookup works normally. This is a limit of the published data rather than of the search.

faqs.q: Are the claim boundaries accurate enough to stake from?
faqs.a: No. Published boundaries are for visualization and planning. They are not legal surveys, precision varies by source, and they should never be used to determine an exact boundary. Use the responsible registry for anything that turns on where a line actually falls.
